title: Subquery vs Join
description: Rewrite correlated subqueries as JOINs for better performance

data.text: Correlated subqueries run once per outer row, often causing N+1-like behavior at the SQL level. Rewriting them as JOINs or using window functions can dramatically improve performance.

data.title: Subquery anti-patterns
items: Subquery in WHERE with IN and EXISTS

data.title: Correlated subquery
data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
  (SELECT MAX(o.total)
   FROM orders o
   WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS max_order
FROM customers c;

data.title: Rewritten as LEFT JOIN
data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, MAX(o.total) AS max_order
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

data.title: Tip
data.text: Window functions often replace both correlated subqueries and complex self-joins for ranking and running totals.

items.question: Are subqueries always slow?
items.answer: No. Non-correlated subqueries can be materialized efficiently. Correlated subqueries are the main concern.

items.question: When should I use EXISTS?
items.answer: Use EXISTS when you only need to check existence and do not need columns from the subquery.

items.question: Can the optimizer rewrite subqueries?
items.answer: Some databases transform subqueries to joins automatically, but do not rely on it.

data.title: Summary
points: Correlated subqueries execute per outer row
Rewrite as JOINs or window functions
data.takeaway: Subqueries are readable but often expensive. Prefer set-based JOINs and window functions for performance.
